# The footer's path is a claim by whoever sealed the object, so a legitimately
# sealed object dropped in at another path used to merge happily - the driver
# decrypted whatever it was handed. Both sides of the footer are now checked
# against the incoming branch's own audit log.

exec git init
exec git config user.email test@sesam.dev
exec git config user.name 'Sesam Test'

cp a.txt $TMPDIR/a.txt
cp b.txt $TMPDIR/b.txt
cp a2.txt $TMPDIR/a2.txt

exec sesam init --user admin --install-merge
exec git add -A
exec git commit -m 'init sesam'

cp $TMPDIR/a.txt a
cp $TMPDIR/b.txt b
exec sesam add a --group admin
exec sesam add b --group admin
exec git add -A
exec git commit -m 'add a and b'

# ATTACKER: put b's (properly signed) object at a's path, without touching the
# audit log, and bypass our hooks the way any plain git client would.
exec git checkout -b evil
cp .sesam/objects/b.sesam .sesam/objects/a.sesam
exec git add .sesam/objects/a.sesam
exec git commit --no-verify -m 'evil: b object at a path'

# OURS: change a legitimately, so git has to merge that object.
exec git checkout master
cp $TMPDIR/a2.txt a
exec sesam seal
exec git add -A
exec git commit -m 'ours: reseal a'

# Refused: verifying the incoming branch as a whole catches it before anything
# is decrypted, because the object no longer answers for the path it sits at.
! exec git merge evil
stderr 'a: missing \.sesam file'
stderr 'does not verify - refusing to merge it'

# Our own content is untouched.
exec cat a
stdout 'A-SECOND'

-- a.txt --
A-FIRST
-- b.txt --
B-ONLY
-- a2.txt --
A-SECOND
